chapter.name: Sciatica / Lumbosacral Radicular Syndrome
chapter.oneLine: Leg-dominant neural pain from lumbosacral nerve-root irritation/compression; localize clinically first, image when the result is expected to change management or when red flags/neurological loss demand it.
definition: Sciatica is a clinical syndrome of radiating leg pain arising from a lumbosacral nerve-root disorder.
Radicular pain = pain generated by root irritation/inflammation.
Radiculopathy = objective loss of root function such as weakness, sensory deficit or reflex change.
Most classic lower-limb sciatica is L5 or S1 related.

terminology.meaning: Clinical syndrome; not a single pathology.
Pain attributed to a lumbar/sacral root.
Objective neurological dysfunction in a root distribution.
Structural diagnosis that may or may not explain symptoms.

appliedAnatomy.clinical: Paracentral/lateral-recess lesion commonly affects traversing L5 root.
Paracentral/lateral-recess lesion commonly affects traversing S1 root.
Foraminal/far-lateral lesion usually affects the exiting root.
Highly pain-sensitive; foraminal compression can produce severe neural pain.
Degenerative hypertrophy contributes to lateral-recess/foraminal/central stenosis.
Peripheral sciatic neuropathy can mimic radiculopathy; localization differs.

epidemiology.data: Published estimates vary widely because case definitions differ; first-time incidence studies range from <1% to 37%.
epidemiology.takeHome: Never quote one universal prevalence without defining the population.

epidemiology.data: Classic literature commonly estimates a minority have true sciatica/radicular syndrome.
epidemiology.takeHome: Most low-back pain is not sciatica.

epidemiology.data: Lumbar disc herniation is the dominant classic cause, but stenosis, spondylolisthesis, tumor, infection and mimics matter.
epidemiology.takeHome: Do not stop differential reasoning after seeing a disc bulge.

epidemiology.data: No single robust nationwide sciatica prevalence figure is established.
epidemiology.takeHome: Local studies should be labeled local, not national.

epidemiology.data: Disc-related radiculopathy is common in working-age/middle-aged adults; degenerative stenotic syndromes increase with age.
epidemiology.takeHome: Age changes the likely mechanism and imaging differential.

epidemiology.data: Sex associations are inconsistent across studies.
epidemiology.takeHome: Avoid teaching a fixed male:female ratio.

occupationalRisk.evidence: Associated with increased sciatica risk in occupational cohorts.
occupationalRisk.clinical: Ask about load, frequency, technique and recovery time.

occupationalRisk.evidence: Relevant in drivers/heavy-equipment operators, especially with obesity in some cohorts.
Certain industrial occupations show higher hospitalization risk.
Systematic reviews identify them as modifiable risk factors.
occupationalRisk.clinical: Frame as recovery/global-health modifiers, not blame.

etiology: Lumbar disc herniation: protrusion, extrusion or sequestration.
Lateral recess or foraminal stenosis from disc/facet/osteophyte/ligamentum flavum change.
Less common: tumor, infection, epidural collection/hematoma, fracture, inflammatory disease.
Non-spinal mimics: hip/SI pathology, vascular claudication, peripheral nerve entrapment, polyneuropathy.

pathophysiology.explanation: Root compression narrows neural space and impairs conduction.
Disc material can trigger cytokine-mediated root inflammation; severe pain may occur with modest compression.
Severe canal/foraminal compromise can impair root microcirculation.
Produces shooting pain, paresthesia and allodynia.
Produces objective weakness, sensory loss, reflex reduction and possible denervation.

clinicalPatterns.clues: Leg-dominant pain, cough/sneeze strain provocation, positive SLR, younger/middle age.
Walking/standing provokes; sitting/flexion relieves; think central/lateral recess stenosis.
Weakness/foot drop may exceed pain severity.

history: Exact pain map from back/buttock to thigh, leg, foot and toes.
Is leg pain greater than back pain? Does it extend below the knee?
Duration and trajectory: improving, stable or worsening.
Weakness, foot slap/drop, heel-walk or toe-walk difficulty.
Walking distance/time to symptoms and posture-related relief.
Bladder retention/incontinence, bowel dysfunction, saddle/genital numbness.
Cancer, fever, immunosuppression, weight loss, night pain.
Occupation: lifting, whole-body vibration, prolonged driving/sitting.
Prior imaging, injections, surgery and treatment response.
Medication safety: ulcer/GI bleed, CKD, CVD/BP, anticoagulants, pregnancy, allergy.

examSequence.items: Posture/list, gait, foot slap/drop, muscle wasting, sit-to-stand.
Flexion, extension, side-bending; centralization/peripheralization where used.
SLR, Crossed SLR, Slump; Bragard sensitization; Bowstring modification.
Knee extension, dorsiflexion, EHL, eversion, plantar flexion, repeated heel rise.
L4 medial leg/ankle; L5 dorsum/great toe; S1 lateral foot/sole.
Heel walk; toe walk; repeated single-leg heel raise.
Hip, SI, pulses/vascular, common peroneal, femoral nerve/upper lumbar roots.

specialTests.how: Supine passive hip flexion with knee extended; note angle and exact symptoms.
specialTests.positive: Concordant radicular pain, typically below knee, commonly 30–70°.
specialTests.meaning: Supports L5/S1 root irritation; sensitive but not highly specific.
specialTests.limitation: Hamstring/posterior-thigh stretch alone is not a positive radicular test.
specialTests.next: Correlate with motor, sensory, reflex and imaging need.

specialTests.meaning: Lower sensitivity, higher specificity for disc herniation/root compression.
specialTests.limitation: Negative test does not exclude radiculopathy.
specialTests.next: Raises confidence when other findings agree.

specialTests.how: Seated spinal flexion + knee extension + ankle dorsiflexion with sensitization/release.
specialTests.positive: Concordant neural symptoms altered by sensitizing maneuvers.

specialTests.how: After SLR symptoms appear, lower leg slightly then dorsiflex ankle.
After SLR symptoms, flex knee slightly and apply pressure over tibial nerve/popliteal fossa.
specialTests.meaning: Historical adjunct for sciatic nerve tension.
specialTests.limitation: Less commonly used; limited modern diagnostic evidence.

specialTests.test: Femoral nerve stretch / prone knee bend

slrAngleLogic.interpretation: Very early symptom reproduction = high irritability possible, but nonspecific.
slrAngleLogic.severity: Do NOT label as severe disc prolapse from angle alone.
slrAngleLogic.next: Recheck technique; correlate with deficit/red flags.

slrAngleLogic.interpretation: Classical positive range for concordant lower-limb radicular pain.
slrAngleLogic.severity: Useful diagnostic clue, not a severity grade.

slrAngleLogic.interpretation: Less specific for nerve-root tension; hip/hamstring/SI/local sources become more important.
slrAngleLogic.severity: Not 'mild sciatica' simply because angle is high.

neurologicSeverity.meaning: Symptom burden only; not urgency alone.

neurologicSeverity.high: Falls, heel/toe walk failure, marked gait loss

rootLocalization.special: Femoral stretch more useful than SLR.

rootLocalization.function: Heel-walk difficulty, toe drag, foot drop
rootLocalization.special: Weak inversion favors radiculopathy over isolated common-peroneal neuropathy.
Compare calf bulk and repeated heel raises.

symptomToLocalization.meaning: Root irritation more likely if distribution is concordant and below knee.
Sensory irritation; weak level specificity alone.
More useful for localization than vague paresthesia.
Myotomal dysfunction; more important than pain severity.
symptomToLocalization.do: MRC grade and repeat over time.

symptomToLocalization.meaning: Often L5 radiculopathy or common-peroneal neuropathy; also plexus/central causes.
symptomToLocalization.do: Test dorsiflexion, EHL, inversion, eversion, sensory pattern.
Correlate Achilles reflex and lateral-foot sensation.

differential.clue: Foot drop; inversion often preserved; fibular-head tenderness/Tinel may exist.
Wider tibial + peroneal deficits; hamstring involvement depending level.
Groin pain, reduced internal rotation, hip provocative tests.
Provocation cluster; no objective root deficit.
Pulse/ABI abnormalities; symptoms less dependent on spinal flexion.
Bilateral length-dependent sensory loss; distal reflex changes.
Pure lateral-thigh sensory syndrome; no motor/reflex loss.

labTests.when: Febrile suspected spinal infection before antibiotics when feasible

labTests.helps: Treatable neuropathy differential; not routine classic unilateral sciatica.

investigationTimeline.reason: ACR rates routine initial radiography/MRI usually not appropriate without red flags.

investigationTimeline.scenario: Trauma / osteoporosis / older age / chronic steroids

xray.meaning: Degenerative disc disease; indirect/nonspecific. Does not prove root compression.
Spondylosis; may contribute to foraminal narrowing.
Can contribute to lateral recess/foraminal stenosis.
Does not exclude disc herniation or root compression.

mri.clinical: Common; significance depends on actual root/recess/foramen compromise.
Greater extension beyond base; often has higher spontaneous-resorption tendency.
Free fragment; migration possible; can cause acute severe syndrome.
Neurogenic claudication/multiroot pattern more likely than isolated single-root pain.
Most meaningful when side/level matches neurological exam.
Not a standalone explanation for radiculopathy.

otherImaging.when: Fracture, pars defect, bony stenosis, calcification; when MRI unavailable/contraindicated in selected cases.
otherImaging.limitation: Inferior to MRI for routine root/disc soft-tissue assessment.

otherImaging.when: Selected preoperative problem-solving when MRI contraindicated/nondiagnostic.
Localization uncertain, symptoms persist, or peripheral nerve/plexus differential competes.
otherImaging.limitation: Timing matters; early studies may be nondiagnostic.

conservativeTreatment.plan: Education; activity within tolerance; avoid prolonged bed rest; individualized short NSAID trial if appropriate; symptom-guided rehab.
Progress walking, trunk/hip conditioning and neural/mobility work as tolerated; repeat neurological exam.
MRI if intervention/surgery likely; shared decision about epidural/surgical opinion.

drugMatrix.examples: Ibuprofen, diclofenac; selected COX-2 inhibitor by risk/label
drugMatrix.evidence: NICE: limited evidence of benefit in sciatica; lowest effective dose for shortest duration.
drugMatrix.safety: GI, renal, hepatic, cardiovascular/BP, anticoagulants, pregnancy, hypersensitivity; avoid duplicate NSAIDs.

drugMatrix.role: Not a sciatica-specific or 'latest better' drug; may be chosen for another licensed pain/inflammatory context after individualized risk assessment.
drugMatrix.evidence: Current SmPC indications do not include sciatica; cardiovascular risk increases with dose/duration.
drugMatrix.safety: Avoid active GI bleed, severe renal dysfunction, significant CV disease/uncontrolled hypertension per product labeling; use lowest dose/shortest time.

drugMatrix.evidence: Placebo-controlled trial found no significant leg-pain/functional benefit and more adverse events; NICE advises against gabapentinoids for sciatica.
drugMatrix.safety: Sedation, dizziness, edema, misuse/dependence; renal adjustment.

drugMatrix.evidence: NICE advises against gabapentinoids/other antiepileptics for sciatica.
Trial evidence shows modest function but no meaningful pain benefit; NICE advises against oral corticosteroids for sciatica.
drugMatrix.safety: Hyperglycemia, infection, mood, GI, bone effects.

drugMatrix.role: Consider only if meaningful acute muscle spasm coexists; evidence pertains more to acute non-radicular LBP than true sciatica.
Not a sciatica-specific treatment; not recommended alone for low-back pain by NICE.
Treat documented/suspected deficiency or appropriate neuropathy.
drugMatrix.evidence: Does not mechanically decompress a nerve root.

drugMatrix.role: Avoid chronic sciatica prescribing; acute role remains uncertain and should be exceptional.
drugMatrix.evidence: NICE: do not offer opioids for chronic sciatica.

interventions.expected: Short-term symptom reduction in selected patients.
interventions.avoid: Not for neurogenic claudication from central canal stenosis under NICE; not a substitute for emergency decompression.

interventions.expected: May help localize or temporarily relieve symptoms.
interventions.avoid: Do not treat response as perfect proof of diagnosis.

interventions.indication: Persistent disabling concordant radiculopathy despite reasonable non-surgical care; earlier for significant/progressive motor deficit.
interventions.expected: Usually faster leg-pain relief in selected patients.
interventions.avoid: Do not operate on imaging abnormality alone.

interventions.indication: Cauda equina syndrome or rapidly progressive major neurological compromise.
interventions.avoid: Do not delay for prolonged conservative trial.

interventions.indication: Selected instability/deformity/other structural indication, not routine primary sciatica surgery.

surgeryDecision.criteria: No CES, no significant/progressive motor deficit, tolerable/improving trajectory.
surgeryDecision.action: Education + activity + rehab + cautious symptom medication.

surgeryDecision.criteria: Objective weakness, foot drop, progressive deficit, severe refractory functional loss.
Persistent disabling radicular pain, non-surgical treatment failed, imaging matches symptoms.
CES or rapidly progressive major neurological deficit.

prognosis: Most acute disc-related sciatica improves over time with non-surgical care.
Spontaneous disc resorption is common, particularly with extruded/sequestered fragments.
Surgery generally provides faster relief in appropriately selected persistent disc-herniation sciatica; long-term differences narrow.
Progressive neurological deficit, long symptom duration, severe baseline disability and important work/psychosocial barriers may worsen recovery.

followUp.who: Severe pain, early objective weakness or diagnostic uncertainty
followUp.check: Motor power, sensory/reflex changes, bladder/bowel/saddle symptoms, medication tolerance.
Pain distribution, SLR/neurodynamic response, gait, activity and medication adverse effects.
Objective neurological trend, disability, need for MRI if management may change.

outcomeMeasures: NRS/VAS leg pain separately from back pain.
MRC motor grade and heel/toe functional tests.

lifestyle.why: Promotes deconditioning and slower functional recovery.

lifestyle.advice: Temporarily modify heavy lifting/twisting during high irritability
lifestyle.why: Reduces repeated provocation while preserving general activity.
Long-term avoidance can reinforce disability; return should be task-specific.
Smoking is associated with sciatica risk and poorer spinal/surgical outcomes.
Reduces global mechanical/metabolic burden; not a stand-alone explanation for pain.
Diet does not decompress a nerve root; treat diabetes, obesity, B12 deficiency or bone-health indications specifically.

rapidRecall: Pain alone localizes poorly; pain + sensory + motor + reflex localizes much better.
L4–L5 paracentral → usually L5. L5–S1 paracentral → usually S1.
Heel walk = dorsiflexor/L5-predominant screen. Toe walk/heel rise = S1.
SLR is more sensitive; crossed SLR is more specific.
Normal X-ray does not exclude disc herniation.
MRI should answer a management question, not merely document degeneration.
Foot drop is a localization problem and an urgency problem, not just a pain problem.
Pregabalin/gabapentin and oral steroids are not routine guideline-supported sciatica therapy.
Conservative first unless major/progressive neurological loss, CES or another serious cause changes urgency.
